head.citation-title: Calcium phase evolution and strength development in lime-treated soil under controlled carbonation conditions
head.abstracts: © 2026 Elsevier LtdCarbonation has a significant influence on the time-dependent mechanical behavior of lime-treated soil (LTS), yet its interaction with pozzolanic reactions remains inadequately understood. This study investigates the coupled effects of carbonation and pozzolanic reactions, focusing on calcium transformation and strength evolution within LTS. A series of controlled experiments were conducted under different CO₂ concentrations (2% and 20%), carbonation durations (3, 12, and 24 h), and curing periods (7–90 days) to evaluate their effects on unconfined compressive strength (UCS), calcium phase transition, and physicochemical properties. The exchangeable calcium (CE), carbonated calcium (CCA), and total calcium were quantified using EDTA titration, gasometric analysis, and strong acid extraction to elucidate calcium transformation mechanisms. The results reveal that the carbonation progresses inward from the exposed surface, with the highest CCA accumulation occurring at the top and significantly lower levels in the middle and bottom layers. The continuous formation of C-(A)-S-H densifies the soil matrix, enhancing strength while limiting CO₂ penetration, which substantially reduces carbonation efficiency in long-cured specimens. Additionally, carbonation significantly alters the physicochemical properties of LTS by reducing pH, electrical conductivity, and salinity, while increasing resistivity. Meanwhile, the formation of CaCO₃ fills pore spaces, enhances compaction, and improves strength, especially under high CO₂ concentrations that accelerate calcium transformations. Notably, the interplay between carbonation and pozzolanic reactions exhibits both competitive and synergistic characteristics. Early-age carbonation consumes a large portion of CE, suppressing subsequent pozzolanic reactions and subsequent strength development. However, when carbonation occurs after sufficient pozzolanic progress, the decalcification of C-(A)-S-H gels facilitates CCA formation and even enhances strength through matrix.

coredata.dc:description: Carbonation has a significant influence on the time-dependent mechanical behavior of lime-treated soil (LTS), yet its interaction with pozzolanic reactions remains inadequately understood. This study investigates the coupled effects of carbonation and pozzolanic reactions, focusing on calcium transformation and strength evolution within LTS. A series of controlled experiments were conducted under different CO₂ concentrations (2% and 20%), carbonation durations (3, 12, and 24 h), and curing periods (7–90 days) to evaluate their effects on unconfined compressive strength (UCS), calcium phase transition, and physicochemical properties. The exchangeable calcium (CE), carbonated calcium (CCA), and total calcium were quantified using EDTA titration, gasometric analysis, and strong acid extraction to elucidate calcium transformation mechanisms. The results reveal that the carbonation progresses inward from the exposed surface, with the highest CCA accumulation occurring at the top and significantly lower levels in the middle and bottom layers. The continuous formation of C-(A)-S-H densifies the soil matrix, enhancing strength while limiting CO₂ penetration, which substantially reduces carbonation efficiency in long-cured specimens. Additionally, carbonation significantly alters the physicochemical properties of LTS by reducing pH, electrical conductivity, and salinity, while increasing resistivity. Meanwhile, the formation of CaCO₃ fills pore spaces, enhances compaction, and improves strength, especially under high CO₂ concentrations that accelerate calcium transformations. Notably, the interplay between carbonation and pozzolanic reactions exhibits both competitive and synergistic characteristics. Early-age carbonation consumes a large portion of CE, suppressing subsequent pozzolanic reactions and subsequent strength development. However, when carbonation occurs after sufficient pozzolanic progress, the decalcification of C-(A)-S-H gels facilitates CCA formation and even enhances strength through matrix.
